skills: 5.2.1: Design and implement advanced fine-tuning methods
questions.question:
The operations team is designing a fine-tuning pipeline in Azure AI Foundry for a customer support model. The model must be adapted to respond in a specific brand tone while handling multi-turn conversations. The team wants to apply best practices that prevent the model from forgetting general language knowledge and ensure training data quality before the fine-tuning job starts.

Which TWO actions should be included in the pipeline design?

choices.text: Validate training data against the required JSONL schema and review sample conversations for tone consistency before uploading files to Azure AI Foundry.
choices.explanation: Pre-validating training data catches formatting errors and quality issues before the fine-tuning job begins, preventing wasted compute and ensuring the model learns from correctly structured, on-tone examples.

choices.text: Use a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method such as LoRA to update only a small subset of model weights, preserving the base model's general language capabilities.
choices.explanation: Parameter-efficient methods like LoRA freeze most base weights, which directly addresses the requirement to prevent catastrophic forgetting of general language knowledge while still adapting tone and style.

choices.text: Enable continuous fine-tuning on live production traffic by streaming user conversations directly into the training job as new data becomes available.
choices.explanation: Streaming production traffic directly into a live fine-tuning job is not a supported or recommended pattern in Azure AI Foundry. It bypasses quality review and risks poisoning the model with unvetted data.

choices.text: Disable the base model's system prompt handling entirely to reduce interference between the brand tone instructions and the original pre-training objectives.
choices.explanation: Disabling system prompt handling is not a configurable option in Azure OpenAI or AI Foundry fine-tuning, and doing so would break multi-turn conversation structure rather than improving tone alignment.

choices.text: Fine-tune on a single-turn question-answer dataset only, then apply a separate post-processing script to convert single-turn outputs into multi-turn conversation format at inference time.
choices.explanation: Converting single-turn outputs to multi-turn format via post-processing does not teach the model to handle conversational context. Multi-turn examples must be included in the training data for the model to learn that behavior.

questions.tip: Consider what happens before training starts and which training method protects existing model knowledge.
questions.explanation:
Validating data quality upfront and using a parameter-efficient method are the two pillars of a well-designed fine-tuning pipeline that meets both quality and knowledge-retention goals.

**Why they work:** Data validation prevents format errors and ensures brand-tone consistency. LoRA-style methods freeze base weights so general language knowledge is not degraded.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Streaming production traffic: Bypasses quality control and is not a supported Azure AI Foundry pattern.
- Disabling system prompt handling: Not configurable; would break multi-turn conversation structure.
- Post-processing single-turn outputs: Does not teach the model conversational context - that requires multi-turn training data.

questions.question: Arrange the following steps in the correct order to fine-tune a base model in Azure OpenAI and deploy the result for inference.

choices.text: Prepare and validate the training dataset in JSONL format, ensuring each example follows the chat completions message structure.
choices.explanation: Training data must be correctly formatted and validated before it can be uploaded. Errors in the dataset structure will cause the fine-tuning job to fail or produce poor results.

choices.text: Upload the validated training file to Azure OpenAI using the Files API or Azure AI Foundry portal and record the returned file ID.
choices.explanation: The file must be uploaded and assigned a file ID before it can be referenced in a fine-tuning job creation request.

choices.text: Create a fine-tuning job referencing the uploaded file ID, the chosen base model, and any hyperparameter overrides such as number of epochs.
choices.explanation: The fine-tuning job is submitted after the file is available. The job orchestrates training and produces a fine-tuned model artifact when complete.

choices.text: Deploy the completed fine-tuned model to an Azure OpenAI deployment endpoint by creating a new deployment that references the fine-tuned model name.
choices.explanation: Once the fine-tuning job status shows succeeded and a fine-tuned model name is available, a deployment must be created before the model can serve inference requests.

questions.tip: Think about the dependency chain: each step produces an artifact that the next step requires.
questions.explanation:
The Azure OpenAI fine-tuning workflow has a strict dependency order. Training data must be formatted and valid before upload; the file ID returned by the upload is required to create the job; the fine-tuned model name produced by the completed job is required to create a deployment. Skipping or reordering any step prevents the subsequent step from proceeding.

Data preparation comes first because format errors discovered later waste compute. The Files API upload must precede job creation because the job references the file by ID. Deployment is the final step because it requires the fine-tuned model artifact that only exists after the job completes.

skills: 5.2.2: Create and manage synthetic data for fine-tuning
questions.question:
You are preparing a fine-tuning dataset for a GPT-4o mini model that will assist insurance agents with policy interpretation questions. Collecting real customer conversations is not possible due to privacy regulations, and the team has only 50 manually authored seed examples. The dataset must reach at least 500 examples to achieve adequate fine-tuning coverage.

Which approach BEST addresses the data volume requirement while complying with the privacy constraint?

choices.text: Use a capable model such as GPT-4o to generate synthetic question-and-answer pairs grounded in the seed examples, then review and filter the generated examples for accuracy and policy alignment before adding them to the training set.
choices.explanation: Generating synthetic data with a larger model seeded from curated examples is the standard technique for expanding fine-tuning datasets when real data is unavailable or restricted. Human review ensures quality and domain accuracy before the data is used for training.

choices.text: Apply simple text augmentation techniques such as synonym replacement and sentence shuffling to the 50 seed examples to programmatically multiply the dataset to 500 entries.
choices.explanation: Synonym replacement and sentence shuffling can produce grammatically incorrect or semantically altered examples that degrade fine-tuning quality. These techniques do not generate new question-answer reasoning patterns and can introduce noise rather than meaningful diversity.

choices.text: Scrape publicly available insurance forums and Q&A websites for conversation threads, anonymize the text using Azure AI Language PII detection, then add the cleaned text directly to the training set.
choices.explanation: Publicly scraped data introduces uncontrolled quality, domain drift, and potential copyright issues. Even after PII removal, the content may not align with the organization's specific policy interpretation task, and the approach does not address the volume gap reliably.

choices.text: Fine-tune the model on the original 50 examples with an increased epoch count of 20 to compensate for the small dataset size, allowing the model to overfit sufficiently to the task domain.
choices.explanation: Intentional overfitting on 50 examples does not produce a generalizable model. Extreme epoch counts on tiny datasets cause the model to memorize training examples rather than learning transferable task behavior, resulting in poor performance on unseen inputs.

questions.tip: Consider which method generates new, valid training examples without relying on restricted real data.
questions.explanation:
Synthetic data generation using a capable foundation model is the recommended approach in Azure AI Foundry when privacy constraints prevent collecting real data. Seeding generation from curated examples grounds the synthetic data in the correct domain, and human review filters low-quality outputs.

**Why it works:** A larger model can generalize from seed examples to produce diverse, coherent Q&A pairs that cover the training distribution without exposing private information.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Text augmentation: Produces shallow variations without new reasoning patterns; can introduce semantic errors.
- Scraping public forums: Uncontrolled quality and domain alignment; potential copyright and privacy issues.
- Overfitting on 50 examples: Leads to memorization rather than generalization; does not solve the volume problem.

skills: 5.2.2: Create and manage synthetic data for fine-tuning
questions.question:
During a data quality review, the team discovers that 30% of the synthetic fine-tuning examples generated for a customer service model contain factually incorrect product specifications. The full dataset has 2,000 examples stored in Azure Blob Storage and referenced in an Azure AI Foundry data asset. The team needs to remove all incorrect examples and re-upload a cleaned version before the next fine-tuning job runs.

Which sequence of actions correctly updates the training dataset?

choices.text: Filter and remove the incorrect examples from the local JSONL file, upload the cleaned file to Azure Blob Storage, then create a new version of the data asset in Azure AI Foundry pointing to the updated file.
choices.explanation: Creating a new data asset version preserves the history of the original dataset while making the cleaned file available for the next fine-tuning job. This is the correct versioning pattern in Azure AI Foundry.

choices.text: Filter and remove the incorrect examples from the local JSONL file, upload the cleaned file to Azure Blob Storage, then overwrite the existing data asset in Azure AI Foundry in place without creating a new version.
choices.explanation: Overwriting the existing data asset in place without versioning destroys traceability. If the cleaned dataset later proves to have issues, there is no way to recover the previous state or audit what changed.

choices.text: Delete the incorrect examples directly from Azure Blob Storage using Azure Storage Explorer, then trigger the existing fine-tuning job again without modifying the data asset reference.
choices.explanation: Deleting blobs directly while the data asset reference remains unchanged can leave the fine-tuning job pointing at an incomplete or inconsistent file, and does not update the data asset to reflect the corrected content.

choices.text: Tag the incorrect examples with a 'flagged' label in the JSONL metadata field, re-upload the file with flags intact, then configure the fine-tuning job to skip flagged examples during training.
choices.explanation: Azure OpenAI fine-tuning does not support per-example skip flags in the JSONL format. The training job processes all examples in the uploaded file without filtering based on custom metadata fields.

questions.tip: Focus on how Azure AI Foundry manages dataset history and how fine-tuning jobs reference data assets.
questions.explanation:
The correct approach is to produce a cleaned JSONL file, upload it to Blob Storage, and register a new version of the data asset in Azure AI Foundry. This preserves the original dataset for audit purposes while providing the fine-tuning job with a clean, versioned reference.

**Why it works:** Azure AI Foundry data asset versioning is designed for exactly this pattern - new versions track lineage without destroying previous states.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Overwriting in place: Destroys dataset lineage and auditability.
- Deleting blobs directly: Leaves data asset references inconsistent; does not update the registered asset.
- Flagging in JSONL metadata: Azure OpenAI fine-tuning does not honor per-example metadata flags to skip examples.

skills: 5.2.2: Create and manage synthetic data for fine-tuning
questions.question:
Management has decided that all synthetic training data generated for fine-tuning internal models must be auditable, versioned, and reusable across multiple future projects. The data pipeline produces JSONL files in Azure Blob Storage, and different teams may generate synthetic data from different seed corpora.

Which TWO practices should be adopted to satisfy these governance and reusability requirements?

choices.text: Register each generated JSONL file as a versioned data asset in Azure AI Foundry, including metadata that captures the seed dataset, generation model, and date of creation.
choices.explanation: Registering data as versioned assets in Azure AI Foundry provides centralized discovery, lineage tracking, and version history. The metadata fields enable future teams to understand how each dataset was produced and select appropriate versions for reuse.

choices.text: Apply a consistent naming convention to Blob Storage containers that encodes the project name, generation date, and seed corpus identifier, and enforce this convention using Azure Policy.
choices.explanation: A governed naming convention enforced by Azure Policy ensures that all teams produce discoverable, consistently organized data assets. This complements data asset registration by making storage-layer discoverability reliable across teams.

choices.text: Store all generated JSONL files in a single flat Blob Storage container shared by all teams, using file size as the primary differentiator between datasets from different seed corpora.
choices.explanation: A flat shared container with file size as the differentiator provides no meaningful audit trail or lineage information. File size is not a reliable identifier and this approach does not scale across teams with different seed corpora.

choices.text: Regenerate synthetic data fresh for each new project using the same seed corpus, discarding previously generated files to avoid storage costs.
choices.explanation: Discarding previously generated files contradicts the auditability and reusability requirements. Regenerating data from scratch for each project also introduces variability between projects that used similar seeds.

choices.text: Encrypt all JSONL files with customer-managed keys in Azure Key Vault and restrict access using private endpoints, then treat each encrypted file as an independent audit artifact.
choices.explanation: Encryption and private endpoints are valid security controls but do not by themselves provide versioning, lineage, or reusability. Treating encrypted files as audit artifacts does not replace structured data asset registration.

questions.tip: Consider how Azure AI Foundry's data management features and storage-layer governance work together to meet audit and reuse goals.
questions.explanation:
Versioned data asset registration in Azure AI Foundry and a policy-enforced naming convention in Blob Storage together provide the lineage, discoverability, and governance needed for auditable, reusable synthetic datasets.

**Why they work:** Data asset versioning tracks what was generated, from what, and when. Naming conventions enforced by Azure Policy ensure all teams follow the same organizational pattern, making cross-project reuse practical.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Flat container with file size differentiator: No audit trail; unreliable and unscalable.
- Discarding previous files: Directly contradicts auditability and reusability requirements.
- Encryption as audit artifact: A security control, not a governance or versioning mechanism.

Some generated answers contain factually incorrect domain information that could mislead the fine-tuned model
The generated dataset is heavily skewed toward one question category, leaving other categories underrepresented
It is unclear which version of the synthetic dataset was used to train a previously deployed model

choices.text: Vary the generation prompt templates and temperature settings to produce more diverse phrasing across synthetic examples

choices.explanation: Targeted generation prompts that specify underrepresented categories directly address class imbalance by increasing the supply of examples where the dataset is thin.

choices.text: Register each synthetic dataset as a versioned data asset in Azure AI Foundry and log the data asset version used in each fine-tuning job
choices.explanation: Versioned data asset registration combined with job-level lineage logging provides a traceable link between a deployed model and the exact dataset version used to train it.

questions.tip: Think about what specific property of the dataset each challenge affects and which technique directly targets that property.
questions.explanation: Each synthetic data challenge requires a targeted mitigation: diversity problems need varied generation parameters; factual errors require verification before training; class imbalance requires stratified generation; and lineage gaps require versioning and job-level audit logging. skills: 5.2.3: Monitor and optimize fine-tuned model performance
questions.question:
Following a board decision to expand a fine-tuned GPT-4o model into production for automated contract summarization, the team needs to establish ongoing monitoring. The model was fine-tuned on 1,800 legal examples and performed well on the held-out evaluation set. After two weeks in production, users report that summary quality has declined noticeably for contracts written in a newer format adopted by a recent regulatory change.

Which monitoring approach MOST directly identifies whether this degradation is caused by distribution shift in the incoming contract data?

choices.text: Configure Azure AI Foundry evaluation runs on a weekly sample of production inputs using the same evaluation dataset and metrics as the original post-training evaluation, then compare metric trends over time.
choices.explanation: Repeated evaluation runs on production input samples using consistent metrics reveal whether model performance is degrading relative to the baseline. Comparing results week over week surfaces distribution shift if newer contract formats produce lower scores.

choices.text: Set up Azure Monitor alerts on token consumption per request and trigger an investigation whenever average token count increases by more than 20% compared to the previous week's baseline.
choices.explanation: Token consumption is an indirect proxy metric that reflects prompt length changes but does not measure output quality or identify distribution shift in the content. Longer contracts do not necessarily indicate quality degradation.

choices.text: Enable diagnostic logging for the Azure OpenAI deployment to capture request and response latency, then analyze latency spikes as a signal of model struggling with new input patterns.
choices.explanation: Latency metrics reflect inference infrastructure performance rather than output quality. A model generating lower-quality summaries for new contract formats would not necessarily show latency spikes.

choices.text: Re-run the original fine-tuning job on the same training dataset with doubled epochs and redeploy the updated model, reasoning that more training will improve resilience to new contract formats.
choices.explanation: Re-training on the original dataset does not address distribution shift because the new contract format is not represented in that data. More epochs would reinforce the original distribution without improving generalization to the new format.

questions.tip: Consider which metric directly measures output quality on production data rather than infrastructure or usage proxy signals.
questions.explanation:
Periodic evaluation runs on production input samples using consistent quality metrics is the recommended approach in Azure AI Foundry for detecting distribution shift. By holding the evaluation methodology constant and running it on live data over time, declining scores indicate that the production input distribution has moved away from what the model was trained on.

**Why it works:** Quality metrics applied consistently to production samples expose degradation that infrastructure metrics cannot surface. Comparing to the post-training baseline makes shift visible.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Token consumption alerts: An indirect usage metric; longer inputs do not correlate directly with output quality degradation.
- Latency logging: Measures infrastructure performance; quality degradation on new content types does not typically affect latency.
- Re-training on original data: Does not include the new format; more epochs on the original distribution cannot teach the model to handle content it has never seen.

skills: 5.2.3: Monitor and optimize fine-tuned model performance
questions.question:
To reduce infrastructure costs, the team is evaluating whether a fine-tuned GPT-4o mini model used for product description generation can be optimized without retraining. The model currently uses a temperature of 0.9, a presence penalty of 0.6, and a max tokens limit of 800. Reviewers have noted that outputs are occasionally verbose and contain repetitive phrases, but the factual content is accurate.

Which inference parameter adjustment is MOST likely to reduce repetition without degrading factual accuracy?

choices.text: Reduce temperature from 0.9 to 0.4 to decrease output randomness, which tends to produce more focused and less repetitive text while retaining the factual content learned during fine-tuning.
choices.explanation: Lowering temperature makes token selection more deterministic. For a fine-tuned model with accurate factual knowledge, lower temperature encourages the model to use its highest-probability tokens, which are typically the factually correct ones, with less wandering into repetitive filler.

choices.text: Increase presence penalty from 0.6 to 1.5 to more aggressively penalize tokens that have already appeared in the output, directly reducing the likelihood of repeated phrases.
choices.explanation: The presence penalty applies a fixed penalty to tokens that have already appeared, directly discouraging repetition regardless of frequency. Raising it from 0.6 to 1.5 strengthens this effect and is the parameter most directly targeted at the observed repetition problem.

choices.text: Reduce max tokens from 800 to 400 to force the model to produce more concise outputs, which will eliminate repetition by cutting off any content generated after the midpoint of the current output.
choices.explanation: Reducing max tokens truncates outputs but does not address the underlying cause of repetition. The model may simply fit the same repetitive pattern into a shorter output, and aggressive truncation risks cutting off factually important content.

choices.text: Set frequency penalty to 2.0 and simultaneously increase temperature to 1.3 to introduce enough randomness to break repetitive patterns while the frequency penalty limits token reuse.
choices.explanation: A frequency penalty of 2.0 combined with temperature 1.3 would introduce competing forces - high randomness from temperature and strong token-reuse suppression from frequency penalty - that can destabilize output coherence and distort factual accuracy.

questions.tip: Think about which parameter is specifically designed to penalize already-seen tokens in a generation.
questions.explanation:
The presence penalty parameter applies a fixed additive penalty to every token that has already appeared at least once in the output, directly reducing the probability of repetition. Raising it from 0.6 to 1.5 targets the specific complaint without changing temperature-driven factual accuracy.

**Why it works:** Presence penalty is purpose-built for repetition reduction. It penalizes all previously seen tokens equally regardless of how many times they appeared, making it effective against phrase-level repetition.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Reducing temperature: Reduces randomness generally but does not directly target repetition; also incorrect as the primary lever for this problem.
- Reducing max tokens: Truncates outputs without fixing the root cause; may cut factual content.
- High frequency penalty with high temperature: Creates conflicting forces that destabilize coherent and accurate output.

skills: 5.2.3: Monitor and optimize fine-tuned model performance
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, the organization has approved a monitoring framework for all fine-tuned models deployed through Azure AI Foundry. The framework must detect both output quality degradation and unexpected increases in inference cost before they impact end users or exceed budget thresholds.

Which TWO monitoring capabilities should be included in the framework?

choices.text: Schedule automated Azure AI Foundry evaluation runs against a fixed golden dataset on a regular cadence and alert when key quality metrics such as coherence or groundedness fall below defined thresholds.
choices.explanation: Regular automated evaluations against a stable golden dataset provide a consistent quality signal over time. Threshold-based alerts trigger before degradation becomes user-visible, satisfying the quality monitoring requirement.

choices.text: Configure Azure Monitor cost alerts on the Azure OpenAI resource to notify the team when projected monthly spend exceeds a set budget, using token consumption metrics as the cost driver.
choices.explanation: Azure Monitor budget alerts on the Azure OpenAI resource track token consumption and associated costs. Setting a threshold alert ensures the team is notified before unexpected cost increases exceed the budget, satisfying the cost monitoring requirement.

choices.text: Enable verbose request logging to capture every prompt and completion payload in Azure Blob Storage, then manually review a random sample of 100 requests each month to assess quality trends.
choices.explanation: Manual monthly sampling does not satisfy the requirement to detect degradation before it impacts users. The latency between degradation onset and the monthly review means users will already be affected by the time the issue is discovered.

choices.text: Replace the fine-tuned model with the latest base model version on a quarterly schedule as a preventive measure, reasoning that newer base models are less likely to produce degraded outputs.
choices.explanation: Replacing a fine-tuned model with a base model on a schedule eliminates the task-specific adaptations provided by fine-tuning. This approach does not monitor performance - it simply discards the fine-tuned model periodically regardless of actual quality.

choices.text: Monitor the p95 latency of the Azure OpenAI deployment endpoint and trigger a retraining job whenever p95 exceeds 3 seconds, treating high latency as a proxy for model quality issues.
choices.explanation: P95 latency reflects infrastructure and load conditions rather than output quality. A fine-tuned model generating poor outputs does not exhibit predictably higher latency, so latency is not a valid quality proxy for triggering retraining.

questions.tip: Consider which capabilities directly measure output quality and which directly measure cost - these are distinct signals requiring distinct tools.
questions.explanation:
Automated evaluation runs on a golden dataset address quality monitoring, and Azure Monitor budget alerts address cost monitoring. Together they cover both dimensions required by the framework.

**Why they work:** Consistent automated evaluation provides early warning of quality drift. Budget alerts on token consumption in Azure Monitor are the native mechanism for cost threshold enforcement on Azure OpenAI resources.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Manual monthly sampling: Too infrequent; users are impacted before the review cycle catches degradation.
- Quarterly base model replacement: Destroys fine-tuning adaptations without measuring whether quality has actually declined.
- Latency as quality proxy: Latency reflects infrastructure load, not output quality; not a valid retraining trigger.
questions.domain: Optimize generative AI systems and model performance

questions.question: Match each observed fine-tuned model behavior to the MOST appropriate optimization action in Azure AI Foundry.

slots.label: The model frequently generates responses that contradict facts stated in the retrieved context documents
Evaluation scores are declining consistently month over month as production input topics have expanded beyond the original training domain
The model produces accurate content but outputs are consistently two to three times longer than the target response length
The model performs well on most inputs but catastrophically fails on a specific newly introduced query category not present in training data

choices.text: Reduce the max tokens parameter and add explicit length instructions to the system prompt to constrain response verbosity without retraining
choices.explanation: Verbose but accurate outputs are typically controllable through inference parameters and system prompt instructions without requiring a new fine-tuning run.

choices.text: Run groundedness evaluation in Azure AI Foundry to quantify the contradiction rate, then add fine-tuning examples that demonstrate correct grounding behavior
choices.explanation: Groundedness evaluation surfaces how often the model contradicts its context. Adding fine-tuning examples that model correct grounding behavior directly addresses the root cause.

choices.text: Collect or generate labeled examples for the new query category, add them to the training dataset, and run an incremental fine-tuning job to extend model coverage
choices.explanation: A new query category requires training data that covers it. Incremental fine-tuning with targeted new examples is the correct approach when an entire category is missing from the model's learned behavior.

choices.text: Expand the fine-tuning dataset to include examples from the new production topics and retrain the model to realign it with the current input distribution
choices.explanation: Gradual domain drift from expanding topics requires retraining with data that covers the new distribution. Without updated training data, the model cannot recover performance on topics it was never trained on.

questions.tip: Consider whether each symptom is addressable through inference configuration alone or requires changes to the model's training data.
questions.explanation: Each symptom requires a different response: verbosity is an inference-layer problem solved with parameter tuning; groundedness failures indicate training data gaps best addressed through targeted fine-tuning with grounding examples; missing query categories require new training data for those categories; and domain drift requires dataset expansion and retraining to realign with the evolved production distribution. Applying a single approach to all four would over-engineer some problems while failing to solve others.

skills: 5.2.4: Manage a fine-tuned model from development through production deployment
questions.question:
A team has a fine-tuned GPT-4o mini model in an Azure OpenAI resource named `aoai-dev` in East US. They want to move the fine-tuned weights to a production resource named `aoai-prod` in West Europe without re-running the fine-tuning job.

Four CLI sequences are proposed. Which correctly exports the model from the development resource and imports it into the production resource?

**Option A**
```bash
az cognitiveservices account deployment export \
  --resource-group rg-dev \
  --name aoai-dev \
  --model-name ft-legal-v1 \
  --format "LoRA"

az cognitiveservices account deployment import \
  --resource-group rg-prod \
  --name aoai-prod \
  --model-name ft-legal-v1 \
  --source "/subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/rg-dev/providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/aoai-dev"
```

**Option B**
```bash
az cognitiveservices account deployment copy \
  --resource-group rg-dev \
  --name aoai-dev \
  --model-name ft-legal-v1 \
  --target-resource aoai-prod \
  --target-resource-group rg-prod
```

**Option C**
```bash
az cognitiveservices account deployment export \
  --resource-group rg-dev \
  --name aoai-dev \
  --model-name ft-legal-v1

az cognitiveservices account deployment import \
  --resource-group rg-prod \
  --name aoai-prod \
  --model-name ft-legal-v1 \
  --source "/subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/rg-dev/providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/aoai-dev"
```

**Option D**
```bash
az cognitiveservices account deployment import \
  --resource-group rg-prod \
  --name aoai-prod \
  --model-name ft-legal-v1 \
  --source "/subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/rg-dev/providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/aoai-prod"
```

choices.text: Option A
choices.explanation: This is the correct two-step sequence: export from the source resource specifying the model name and format, then import into the target resource referencing the source resource path. This moves the fine-tuned weights without re-training.

choices.text: Option B
choices.explanation: `az cognitiveservices account deployment copy` does not exist. Fine-tuned models are moved using the export and import commands, not a single copy command.

choices.text: Option C
choices.explanation: The export command is missing `--format "LoRA"`. Without specifying the format, the export command is incomplete and will fail or export in an unexpected format, preventing a successful import.

choices.text: Option D
choices.explanation: The import references `aoai-prod` (the destination resource) as the source, pointing at the wrong resource. The source must be the development resource `aoai-dev`.

questions.tip: Fine-tuned model migration requires two steps: export then import. The export must specify the format, and the source path in the import must point at the correct resource.
questions.explanation:
The correct approach uses two CLI commands in sequence: first `az cognitiveservices account deployment export` with `--format "LoRA"` on the source resource, then `az cognitiveservices account deployment import` on the target resource referencing the source resource's full ARM path. This transfers the fine-tuned weights to the production resource without re-running training.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `az cognitiveservices account deployment copy` is not a real command.
- Omitting `--format "LoRA"` from the export command makes it incomplete and prevents a successful import.
- Pointing `--source` at the production resource (`aoai-prod`) instead of the development resource (`aoai-dev`) means the import targets the wrong resource.

skills: 5.2.4: Manage a fine-tuned model from development through production deployment
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, the team notes that a fine-tuned model deployment for an internal knowledge base assistant is consuming more provisioned throughput than expected. Usage telemetry shows that 60% of requests are simple factual lookups that do not require the specialized response style introduced by fine-tuning. The remaining 40% are complex multi-step queries that benefit significantly from the fine-tuned behavior.

Which deployment architecture change MOST reduces cost while preserving fine-tuned quality for complex queries?

choices.text: Deploy both the fine-tuned model and the base GPT-4o mini model as separate Azure OpenAI deployments, then implement a router in the application layer that directs simple factual queries to the base model and complex queries to the fine-tuned deployment.
choices.explanation: Routing simple queries to the lower-cost base model and reserving the fine-tuned deployment for complex queries reduces provisioned throughput consumption on the fine-tuned deployment while maintaining quality where fine-tuning provides measurable value.

choices.text: Increase the provisioned throughput units allocated to the fine-tuned model deployment to reduce per-request latency, then implement response caching for the most frequent factual queries to lower effective request volume.
choices.explanation: Increasing provisioned throughput raises cost rather than reducing it. Response caching helps with repeated identical queries but does not address the structural inefficiency of routing all query types through an expensive fine-tuned deployment.

choices.text: Switch the fine-tuned model deployment from provisioned throughput to pay-as-you-go token billing, then rely on Azure's automatic scaling to manage demand spikes across both simple and complex query types.
choices.explanation: Switching to pay-as-you-go may reduce idle cost but increases per-token cost at scale. It also does not address the architectural inefficiency of processing simple queries through a fine-tuned model when a base model would produce equivalent results at lower cost.

choices.text: Retrain the fine-tuned model with a reduced dataset focused exclusively on complex multi-step queries, then redeploy the smaller, more specialized model to reduce inference cost per token.
choices.explanation: Retraining on a reduced dataset changes the model's capabilities. This approach does not reduce the number of requests hitting the fine-tuned deployment - all requests would still be routed to it, and the cost reduction from a smaller dataset is marginal at inference time.

questions.tip: Think about how to separate request types architecturally rather than modifying the model or its resource allocation.
questions.explanation:
Deploying both the base and fine-tuned models separately and routing at the application layer is the standard cost optimization pattern when only a subset of requests benefit from fine-tuning. The base model handles the 60% of simple queries at lower cost, while the fine-tuned model is reserved for the 40% that justify its use.

**Why it works:** Each model handles only the query type it is best suited for. Provisioned throughput on the fine-tuned deployment covers only 40% of the original volume, directly reducing cost.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Increasing provisioned throughput: Raises cost; caching helps marginally but does not solve the root architectural issue.
- Switching to pay-as-you-go: May increase per-token cost at volume; does not change the fact that simple queries are processed through an unnecessarily capable model.
- Retraining on reduced data: Does not reduce request volume to the fine-tuned deployment; cost impact at inference time is negligible.

skills: 5.2.4: Manage a fine-tuned model from development through production deployment
questions.question:
The operations team is establishing a release process for fine-tuned models across development, staging, and production environments. The process must ensure that only evaluated and approved model versions reach production and that any production deployment can be rolled back to the previous version within minutes if issues are detected.

Which TWO practices should be included in the release process to meet these requirements?

choices.text: Maintain a registry of fine-tuned model versions in Azure AI Foundry with their evaluation results and approval status, and gate promotion to production on a documented approval step that references the registry entry.
choices.explanation: A versioned model registry with evaluation results and an explicit approval gate ensures that only evaluated, approved models advance to production. The registry provides the audit trail required by the process.

choices.text: Keep the previous production model deployment active and route it no traffic, then switch traffic back to it using the application-layer routing configuration if the new deployment requires rollback.
choices.explanation: Retaining the previous deployment with zero traffic allows instant rollback by updating the routing configuration, without waiting for a new deployment to be created. This is the standard blue-green pattern for fast rollback.

choices.text: Promote fine-tuned models directly from development to production as soon as the fine-tuning job completes, relying on production monitoring alerts to detect quality issues after deployment.
choices.explanation: Skipping staging evaluation and promoting directly to production contradicts the requirement that only evaluated and approved models reach production. Relying on post-deployment monitoring means users are exposed to unevaluated models.

choices.text: Delete each previous fine-tuned model version from Azure OpenAI after deploying a new version to reduce resource usage and prevent accidental routing to outdated models.
choices.explanation: Deleting the previous model version eliminates the ability to roll back within minutes. Rollback requires the previous model to remain available as a deployment; deletion forces a full retrain or re-import to recover.

choices.text: Run the fine-tuning job directly against the production Azure OpenAI resource to avoid the overhead of managing separate environment resources.
choices.explanation: Running fine-tuning on the production resource risks destabilizing production inference during training, and bypasses the staging and approval process. Fine-tuning jobs consume resource quota that could impact live deployments.

questions.tip: Consider which practices address the approval gate requirement and which address the rollback speed requirement independently.
questions.explanation:
A versioned registry with approval gates satisfies the requirement that only evaluated models reach production. Retaining the previous deployment for instant traffic switchover satisfies the fast rollback requirement.

**Why they work:** The registry creates a controlled promotion path. The retained previous deployment enables rollback in seconds by toggling routing, without any redeployment or retraining.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Direct dev-to-prod promotion: Bypasses evaluation and approval; users are exposed to unevaluated models.
- Deleting previous versions: Eliminates rollback capability; contradicts the minutes-level recovery requirement.
- Fine-tuning on production resource: Risks quota exhaustion and service disruption; bypasses environment isolation.

skills: 5.2.4: Manage a fine-tuned model from development through production deployment
questions.question: Arrange the following steps in the correct order to safely promote a fine-tuned model from staging to production in Azure OpenAI.

choices.text: Run automated evaluation of the fine-tuned model against the staging golden dataset and confirm that all quality metric thresholds are met before proceeding.
choices.explanation: Evaluation must occur first to confirm the model meets quality requirements. Promoting a model that has not been evaluated risks deploying a poor-quality model to production users.

choices.text: Obtain formal approval from the designated model owner or review board, recording the approval decision against the model version in the registry.
choices.explanation: Approval gates follow successful evaluation. The approval step provides a human checkpoint that confirms evaluation results are acceptable and authorizes the promotion to proceed.

choices.text: Export the approved fine-tuned model from the staging Azure OpenAI resource and import it into the production Azure OpenAI resource.
choices.explanation: The model must be transferred to the production resource before a deployment can be created there. Export and import moves the fine-tuned weights without requiring a new training run.

choices.text: Create a new deployment in the production Azure OpenAI resource referencing the imported fine-tuned model, then shift production traffic to the new deployment and monitor for issues.
choices.explanation: Deployment creation and traffic shifting is the final step. Monitoring immediately after the shift enables fast detection of any issues and supports rollback to the previous deployment if needed.

questions.tip: Consider which steps produce the artifacts or authorizations that subsequent steps depend on.
questions.explanation:
The promotion sequence has strict dependencies: evaluation must confirm quality before approval is sought; approval authorizes the transfer; export and import moves the model artifact to the production resource; and deployment creation with traffic shifting is the final action that makes the model available to production users. Performing approval before evaluation would mean approving an unvalidated model. Attempting to create a production deployment before import would fail because the model artifact does not yet exist in the production resource.

Monitoring after the traffic shift completes the promotion by establishing the feedback loop needed to detect and respond to any issues that evaluation did not surface.
